targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-10), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: an open, loose clump of slender, spreading grey-brown stems under the conifers, its paired oval leaves held in flat sprays; pale yellow paired tubular flowers as the leaves open, then pairs of shiny red berries in mid-summer, the leaves pale yellow in fall

description: A deciduous shrub 1-2 m tall with slender, spreading stems that grow in loose clumps. Its oval leaves, up to 8 cm long, sit in pairs along the twigs; pale yellow tubular flowers hang in pairs as the leaves open in late spring, and they ripen into pairs of shiny red berries almost a centimetre across in mid-summer. In the Tetons it grows in the shade of lodgepole pine, Douglas-fir and spruce-fir forest on the moist canyon slopes, where bears and birds eat the berries.

season_notes.winter: Bare, slender grey-brown stems under the snow-loaded conifers.
season_notes.spring: Leaves open as the snow goes, with pale yellow flowers hanging in pairs beneath them.
season_notes.summer: Pairs of red berries in July and August, eaten by black bears and birds; elk browse the leaves.
season_notes.fall: The leaves turn pale yellow and drop; elk still browse the twigs.

range.where: the understory of the lodgepole pine, Douglas-fir and spruce-fir forests of the Teton canyons and Jackson Hole's forested slopes; western North America from British Columbia and Alberta through the Rocky Mountains to Arizona and New Mexico

notes: No Lonicera is in the library; snowberry (the template) is its family's (Caprifoliaceae) deciduous shrub, with the same opposite, simple, oval leaves and a clumped multi-stemmed habit; the card makes Utah honeysuckle taller and looser, with paired yellow flowers and red berries in place of pink bells and white berries. Height 1-2 m, slender spreading branches, clump-forming (FEIS; Wikipedia, the same); USDA PLANTS: mature height 5 ft, multiple stem, erect, rapid growth, summer foliage porous. Leaves oval to oblong, up to 8 cm by 4 cm (Wikipedia), so leaf_size_m 0.05; leaves expand late March to early May and drop in the fall (FEIS). Flowers in pairs, yellow to yellowish-white, up to 1 cm (Wikipedia; PLANTS: yellow, early summer), April-June (FEIS); May-June for the Tetons is the drafter's reading. Berry red, almost 1 cm (Wikipedia; PLANTS: red, summer to fall, persistent); fruits mature June-September (FEIS); July-August for the Tetons is the drafter's reading. Habitat: understory of mature forest on moist open or wooded slopes and canyons; cool lodgepole pine and Douglas-fir habitat types low, dry to moist Engelmann spruce and subalpine fir types higher; tolerates moderate to dense shade and is common under closed canopies (FEIS), hence shade 0.8; often a climax species (Wikipedia). Fire top-kills it and it resprouts slowly from the root crown, a decreaser after fire; in Grand Teton National Park it was more frequent on unburned than burned spruce-fir sites (FEIS), hence disturbed 0.4. Elevation 683-3353 m overall (FEIS; Wikipedia: 300-3400 m, mostly 1200-2400 m); no Wyoming figure was given. The lodgepole, Douglas-fir and spruce-fir placing on the Teton tile is from the brief. Eaters: FEIS names elk (valuable summer and fall browse), white-tailed deer (minor), moose (trace summer and winter forage in Wyoming), grizzly bears (fruit, summer and fall), black bears (summer) and ruffed grouse (summer); Wikipedia says birds and bears eat the fruit. The American robin stands in for the fruit-eating birds; moose, white-tailed deer, grizzly bear and ruffed grouse are not in the library (the library's sooty grouse is a Pacific species, so it is not used). Cover: FEIS rates it fair to good for small mammals and nongame and upland game birds in Utah and Wyoming, poor for elk and pronghorn; the deer mouse, yellow-pine chipmunk and robin stand for those. Colours (the fall yellow included), crown profile, porosity, stems, the shreddy bark, leaf-on months, the flower and berry densities and drawn sizes are the drafter's judgement, not from a source.
